o1.biggest_strength: It builds the whole post around the data. Writing is weighted 50% in the scorecard, the application is a single customer reply, and the hours are given in local cities (Singapore, Manila, Perth) so Asia-Pacific readers see the fit at once.
o1.biggest_mistake: It gives 15% to a conversation score even though interview impression correlated only 0.11. The career-changer welcome is also thinner than it could be, and the post leaves out the data behind dropping experience requirements.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Cut the interview-based weight, welcome career changers by name with the evidence in the post, and give every scorecard line a 1, 3 and 5 in one scannable table.

o2.biggest_strength: The post is candid and warm in the brand's voice. It puts the weekend rotation (about 8 or 9 a year) and the lone overnight work among the hard parts, tells teachers and hospitality staff plainly that their experience counts, and shares the real evidence for dropping experience requirements.
o2.biggest_mistake: Writing gets only 40% and the second application question (a fixing-problems story) is not a writing sample. The post also gives only UTC hours with no local-time translation, and the length probably runs a little over the 1,100-word cap.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Raise the weight on the written reply, make the second application question a second customer reply, add local-time examples for Asia-Pacific, and trim to the word limit.

reason: Both catch the three big signals and get the numbers right. Output 2 sounds more like us, is more honest about the hard parts, welcomes career changers, and has a fuller scorecard with plain 1/3/5 descriptions and a worked reviewer-hours table. Output 1 weights writing more heavily and gives local times, but it is a little thinner on warmth.
